texts.exact_text: The first NINE, undivided, shows its subject, (in the condition indicated by) Míng Yí, flying, but with drooping wings. When the superior man (is revolving) his going away, he may be for three days without eating. Wherever he goes, the people there may speak (derisively of him).
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 36; scan-backed transcription p. 134, line 1

texts.exact_text: The second SIX, divided, shows its subject, (in the condition indicated by) Míng Yí, wounded in the left thigh. He saves himself by the strength of a (swift) horse; and is fortunate.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 36; scan-backed transcription p. 134, line 2

texts.exact_text: The third NINE, undivided, shows its subject, (in the condition indicated by) Míng Yí, hunting in the south, and taking the great chief (of the darkness). He should not be eager to make (all) correct (at once).
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 36; scan-backed transcription p. 134, line 3

texts.exact_text: The fourth six, divided, shows its subject (just) entered into the left side of the belly (of the dark land). (But) he is able to carry out the mind appropriate (in the condition indicated by) Míng Yí, quitting the gate and courtyard (of the lord of darkness).
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 36; scan-backed transcription p. 134, line 4

texts.exact_text: The fifth six, divided, shows how the count of Jī Zǐ fulfilled the condition indicated by Míng Yí. It will be advantageous to be firm and correct.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 36; scan-backed transcription p. 134, line 5

texts.exact_text: The sixth six, divided, shows the case where there is no light, but (only) obscurity. (Its subject) had at first ascended to (the top of) the sky; his future shall be to go into the earth.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 36; scan-backed transcription p. 134, line 6

texts.exact_text:
In this hexagram **䷣** we have the representation of a good and intelligent minister or officer going forward in the service of his country, notwithstanding the occupancy of the throne by a weak and unsympathising sovereign. Hence comes its name of `Míng Yí`(明夷), or `Intelligence Wounded`, that is, injured and repressed. The treatment of the subject shows how such an officer will conduct himself, and maintain his purpose. The symbolism of the figure is treated of in the same way in the first and second Appendixes. [Appendix VI](appendix06s1.md#p-436) merely says that the advance set forth in [35 ䷢](e6998bjin.md) is sure to meet with wounding, and hence [**䷢ Jìn**](e6998bjin.md) is followed by **䷣ Míng Yí**.

Line 1 is strong, and in its right place; -- its subject should be going forward. But the general signification of the hexagram supposes him to be wounded. The wound, however, being received at the very commencement of its action, is but slight. And hence conies the emblem of a bird hurt so as to be obliged to droop its wings. The subject then appears directly as `the superior man`. He sees it to be his course to desist from the struggle for a time, and is so rapt in the thought that he can fast for three days and not think of it. When he does withdraw, opposition follows him; but it is implied that he holds on to his own good purpose.

Line 2 is weak, but also in its right place, and central; giving us the idea of an officer, obedient to duty and the right. His wound in the left thigh may impede his movements, but does not disable him. He finds means to save himself, and maintains his good purpose.

Line 3, strong and in a strong place, is the topmost line of the lower trigram ☲. It responds also to line 6, in which the idea of the sovereign, emblemed by the upper trigram, is concentrated. The lower trigram is the emblem of light or brightness, the idea of which again is expressed by the south, to which we turn when we look at the sun in its meridian height. Hence the subject of the line [becomes a hunter pursuing his game](e5aeb6e4babajiaren.md#p-137), and successfully. The good officer will be successful in his struggle; but let him not be over eager to put all things right at once.

Line 4 is weak, but in its right place. [Zhū Xī](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhu_Xi) says he does not understand the symbolism, as given in the Text. The translation indicates the view of it commonly accepted. The subject of the line evidently escapes from his position of danger with little damage.

Line 5 should be the place of the ruler or sovereign in the hexagram; but 6 is assigned as that place in `Míng Yí`. The officer occupying 5, the centre of the upper trigram **☷**, and near to the sovereign, has his ideal in the count of `Jī Zǐ`([箕子](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jizi)), whose action appears in the [Zhōu Shū](https://ctext.org/dictionary.pl?if=en&id=43059). He is a historical personage.

Line 6 sets forth the fate of the ruler, who opposes himself to the officer who would do him good and intelligent service. Instead of becoming as the sun, enlightening all from the height of the sky, he is as the sun hidden below the earth. I can well believe that the writer had the last king of [Shāng](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shang_dynasty) in his mind.

texts.exact_text: 明夷，利艱貞。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/明夷; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 36, 易經卦辭

texts.exact_text: 明入地中，明夷。內文明而外柔順，以蒙大難，文王以之。利艱貞，晦其明也。內難而能正其志，箕子以之。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/明夷; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 36, 彖

texts.exact_text: 明入地中，明夷。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/明夷; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 36, 大象

texts.exact_text: 初九，明夷于飛，垂其翼，君子于行，三日不食，有攸往，主人有言。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/明夷; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 36, 爻 1

texts.exact_text: 君子于行，義不食也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/明夷; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 36, 小象 1

texts.exact_text: 六二，明夷，夷于左股，用拯馬壯吉。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/明夷; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 36, 爻 2

texts.exact_text: 六二之吉，順以則也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/明夷; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 36, 小象 2

texts.exact_text: 九三，明夷于南狩，得其大首，不可疾貞。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/明夷; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 36, 爻 3

texts.exact_text: 南狩之志，乃得大也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/明夷; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 36, 小象 3

texts.exact_text: 六四，入于左腹，獲明夷之心，于出門庭。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/明夷; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 36, 爻 4

texts.exact_text: 入于左腹，獲心意也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/明夷; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 36, 小象 4

texts.exact_text: 六五，箕子之明夷，利貞。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/明夷; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 36, 爻 5

texts.exact_text: 箕子之貞，明不可息也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/明夷; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 36, 小象 5

texts.exact_text: 上六，不明晦，初登于天，後入于地。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/明夷; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 36, 爻 6

texts.exact_text: 初登于天，照四國也；後入于地，失則也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/明夷; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 36, 小象 6

texts.exact_text:
(The symbol of) the Earth and that of Brightness entering into the midst of it give the idea of ䷣ Míng Yí (Brightness wounded or obscured).

The inner (trigram) denotes being accomplished and bright; the outer, being pliant and submissive.

'It will be advantageous to realise the difficulty (of the position), and maintain firm correctness: -- that is, (the individual concerned) should obscure his brightness. The case of the count of Jī Zǐ was that of one who, amidst the difficulties of his House, was able (thus) to maintain his aim and mind correct.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix I, Hexagram 36, p. 242

texts.exact_text: (The trigram ☷ representing) the earth and ☲ that for the bright (sun) entering within it form ䷣ Míng Yí. The superior man, in accordance with this, conducts his management of men; -- he shows his intelligence by keeping it obscured.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 36, p. 312

texts.exact_text: 'The superior man (is revolving his) going away:' -- (in such a case) he feels it right not to eat.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 36, line 1, p. 312

texts.exact_text: 'The good fortune of (the subject of) the second SIX, divided,' is due to the proper fashion of his acting according to his circumstances.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 36, line 2, p. 312

texts.exact_text: With the aim represented by 'hunting in the south' a great achievement is accomplished.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 36, line 3, p. 312

texts.exact_text: 'He has (just) entered into the left side of the belly (of the dark land):' -- he is still able to carry out the idea in his (inner) mind.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 36, line 4, p. 312

texts.exact_text: 'With the firm correctness of the count of Jī Zǐ,' his brightness could not be (quite) extinguished.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 36, line 5, p. 312

texts.exact_text: 'He had at first ascended to (the top of) the sky:' -- he might have enlightened the four quarters of the kingdom. 'His future shall be to go into the earth:' -- he has failed to fulfil the model (of a ruler).
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 36, line 6, p. 312
